findings.claim: The new lookahead accepts a lone U+20E3 (combining enclosing keycap) or a single Regional Indicator as the "anchor", so strings that are still not valid emoji pass validation.
findings.rationale: `⃣` and Regional Indicators are themselves `\p{Emoji_Component}`, so they satisfy both the lookahead and the main character class. `emoji().test("⃣")` (a bare keycap with no digit/#/* base) and `emoji().test("\u{1F1FA}")` (a single regional indicator, i.e. half a flag) both return true. The stated goal of the lookahead is to require an anchor because components are "not an emoji without a base", but these two anchors have exactly the same base-less problem. Reasonably confident; easy to verify in a REPL.

findings.claim: The fix only requires one pictograph/RI/keycap somewhere in the string; arbitrary ASCII digits, `#`, `*`, ZWJ and variation selectors are still accepted alongside it.
findings.rationale: Because the lookahead is `(?=[\s\S]*...)` and the body class is unchanged, inputs like "\u{1F600}123", "#*\u{1F600}" or "\u{1F600}‍‍‍" still match. The comment implies digits/#/* are no longer acceptable, but they are only rejected when no pictograph appears anywhere in the string. Incomplete fix if the intent was to reject stray components. High confidence on the behavior.

findings.claim: Behavior change: inputs that previously validated (e.g. "123", "#", "*", a lone skin-tone modifier, a lone ZWJ) now fail, which is a breaking change for existing callers.
findings.rationale: This is presumably the intended fix, but `z.string().emoji()` consumers relying on the old looser acceptance will start seeing validation errors, with no version gate or changelog note visible in this hunk. Worth confirming existing emoji test fixtures are updated and that this lands in a suitable release.

findings.claim: `\p{Regional_Indicator}` is a less commonly used Unicode binary property; on an engine that does not recognize it, `new RegExp(_emoji, "u")` throws a SyntaxError at call time rather than at module load.
findings.rationale: Because `emoji()` builds the RegExp lazily, an unsupported property name would surface as a runtime SyntaxError inside user validation. Both properties are ES2018 and supported by modern engines, so this is probably fine, but worth checking against the library's minimum engine/browser support. Low confidence this is an actual problem.
